{{Short description|Term in mathematical logic}}
In [[mathematical logic]], the '''spectrum of a sentence''' is the [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of [[natural number]]s occurring as the size of a [[Finite model theory|finite model]] in which a given [[Sentence (mathematical logic)|sentence]] is true. By a result in [[descriptive complexity]], a set of natural numbers is a spectrum if and only if it can be recognized in [[NE (complexity)|non-deterministic "weak" exponential time (2<sup>O(n)</sup>)]], which is a subclass of NEXP.

==Definition==

Let ''ψ'' be a sentence in [[first-order logic]].  The ''spectrum'' of ''ψ'' is the set of natural numbers ''n'' such that there is a finite model for ''ψ'' with ''n'' elements.

If the vocabulary for ''ψ'' consists only of relational symbols, then ''ψ'' can be regarded as a sentence in [[existential second-order logic]] (ESOL) quantified over the relations, over the empty vocabulary.  A ''generalised spectrum'' is the set of models of an ESOL sentence.

==Examples==

* The spectrum of the [[first-order formula]]
<math>\exists z,o ~ \forall a,b,c ~ \exists d,e</math>
:<math>a+z=a=z+a ~ \land~ a\cdot z=z=z\cdot a ~ \land~ a+d = z</math>
:<math>\land~ a+b = b+a ~ \land~ a\cdot(b+c) = a\cdot b+a\cdot c ~ \land~(a+b)+c=a+(b+c)</math>
:<math>\land~ a \cdot o=a=o \cdot a ~ \land~ a\cdot e=o ~\land~ (a\cdot b)\cdot c=a\cdot (b\cdot c)</math>
is <math>\{p^{n}\mid p \text{ prime}, n \in \mathbb{N}\}</math>, the set of powers of a [[prime number]]. Indeed, with <math>z</math> for <math>0</math> and <math>o</math> for <math>1</math>, this sentence describes the set of [[Field (mathematics)|fields]]; the [[cardinality]] of a [[finite field]] is the power of a prime number.
* The spectrum of the monadic second-order logic formula <math>\exists S, T ~ \forall x ~ \left\{x\in S\iff x\not\in T
 \land~ f(f(x)) = x
 \land~ x \in S \iff f(x) \in T\right\}</math> is the set of [[Parity (mathematics)|even]] numbers. Indeed, <math>f</math> is a [[bijection]] between <math>S</math> and <math>T</math>, and <math>S</math> and <math>T</math> are a partition of the universe. Hence the cardinality of the universe is even.
* The set of finite and co-finite sets is the set of spectra of first-order logic with the successor relation.
* The set of ultimately periodic sets is the set of spectra of monadic second-order logic with a unary function. It is also the set of spectra of monadic second-order logic with the successor function.

==Descriptive complexity==

''[[Fagin's theorem]]'' is a result in [[descriptive complexity|descriptive complexity theory]] that states that the set of all properties expressible in existential [[second-order logic]] is precisely the [[complexity class]] [[NP (complexity class)|NP]]. It is remarkable since it is a characterization of the class NP that does not invoke a model of computation such as a [[Turing machine]].  The theorem was proven by [[Ronald Fagin]] in 1974 (strictly, in 1973 in his doctoral thesis). 

As a corollary, Jones and [[Alan Selman|Selman]] showed that a set is in the complexity class [[NE (complexity)|NE]] if it is a spectrum.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Jones | first1=Neil D. | last2=Selman | first2=Alan L.|author2-link=Alan Selman | title=Turing machines and the spectra of first-order formulas | zbl=0288.02021 | journal=J. Symb. Log. | volume=39 | issue=1 | pages=139–150 | year=1974 | doi=10.2307/2272354 | jstor=2272354 }}</ref>

One direction of the proof is to show that, for every first-order formula <math>\varphi</math>, the problem of determining whether there is a model of the formula of [[cardinality]] ''n'' is equivalent to the [[Boolean satisfiability problem|problem of satisfying a formula]] of size polynomial in ''n'', which is in NP(n) and thus in NE of the input to the problem (the number ''n'' in binary form, which is a string of size log(''n'')).

This is done by replacing every [[existential quantifier]] in <math>\varphi</math> with [[disjunction]] over all the elements in the model and replacing every [[universal quantifier]] with [[logical conjunction|conjunction]] over all the elements in the model. Now every predicate is on elements in the model, and finally every appearance of a predicate on specific elements is replaced by a new propositional variable. Equalities are replaced by their truth values according to their assignments.

For example:

<math>\forall{x} \forall{y} \left(P(x)\wedge P(y)\right)\rightarrow (x=y)</math>

For a model of cardinality 2 (i.e. ''n''= 2) is replaced by

<math>\big(\left(P(a_1)\wedge P(a_1)\right)\rightarrow (a_1=a_1)\big)\wedge \big(\left(P(a_1)\wedge P(a_2)\right)\rightarrow (a_1=a_2)\big)\wedge \big(\left(P(a_2)\wedge P(a_1)\right)\rightarrow (a_2=a_1)\big)\wedge \big(\left(P(a_2)\wedge P(a_2)\right)\rightarrow (a_2=a_2)\big)</math>

Which is then replaced by
<math>\big(\left(p_1\wedge p_1\right)\rightarrow \top\big)\wedge \big(\left(p_1\wedge p_2\right)\rightarrow \bot\big)\wedge \big(\left(p_2\wedge p_1\right)\rightarrow \bot\big)\wedge \big(\left(p_2\wedge p_2\right)\rightarrow \top\big)</math>

where <math>\top</math> is truth, <math>\bot</math> is falsity, and <math>p_1</math>, <math>p_2</math> are propositional variables.
In this particular case, the last formula is equivalent to <math>\neg(p_1\wedge p_2)</math>, which is satisfiable.

The other direction of the proof is to show that, for every set of binary strings accepted by a non-deterministic Turing machine running in exponential time (<math>2^{cx}</math> for input length x), there is a first-order formula <math>\varphi</math> such that the set of numbers represented by these binary strings are the spectrum of <math>\varphi</math>.

Jones and Selman mention that the spectrum of first-order formulas without equality is just the set of all natural numbers not smaller than some minimal cardinality.

===Other properties===

The set of spectra of a theory is closed under [[Union (set theory)|union]], [[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]], addition, and multiplication. In full generality, it is not known if the set of spectra of a theory is closed by complementation; this is the so-called Asser's problem. By the result of Jones and Selman, it is equivalent to the problem of whether NE = co-NE; that is, whether NE is closed under complementation. By Fagin's theorem, this is also equivalent to determining if unary NP and unary Co-NP are the same. To show that the set of first-order spectra is not closed under complementation thus entails showing that P is not equal to NP.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Szwast | first = Wiesław
 | doi = 10.1002/malq.19900360105
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Zeitschrift für Mathematische Logik und Grundlagen der Mathematik
 | mr = 1030536
 | pages = 23–27
 | title = On the generator problem
 | volume = 36
 | year = 1990}}</ref>
